title: A Judge Killed the $100,000 H-1B Fee. Four Days Later, He Froze His Own Ruling.
excerpt: The legal seesaw has left Indian tech workers in limbo as Trump appeals and Congress moves to codify the fee permanently.
body:
A federal judge in Boston has struck down President Donald Trump's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions — and then, four days later, agreed to freeze his own ruling while the administration rushes to an appeals court. The legal whiplash has left hundreds of thousands of Indian tech workers, doctors, and engineers caught between a court victory and a government that refuses to let it stand.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin issued his decision on June 8, calling the fee an unauthorised tax that only Congress has the power to impose. The ruling came in a lawsuit brought by 20 Democratic state attorneys general, led by California, who argued the fee was crippling public hospitals, universities, and school districts that depend on H-1B workers to fill specialised roles.

"The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," Sorokin wrote in a 42-page opinion. He cited the Supreme Court's February ruling that struck down Trump's sweeping tariffs under a similar constitutional logic: the president cannot levy a tax without Congress.

## The Fee's Toll on Indian Workers

The numbers tell a stark story. Since Trump imposed the fee through a September 2025 proclamation, H-1B applications have plunged 27 per cent — from 470,342 to 343,981. As of mid-February, just 85 employers had actually paid the $100,000 charge. Before the proclamation, the typical cost of an H-1B petition ranged from $2,000 to $5,000.

Indians are, by far, the most affected. They account for more than 70 per cent of all approved H-1B petitions annually. The fee effectively priced out smaller employers and Indian IT service firms, which had already seen a 40 per cent drop in H-1B approvals this year.

## Victory, Then a Stay

The relief was short-lived. The Trump administration appealed the ruling on the same day and on June 12 filed an emergency motion asking Sorokin to stay his own order. The Department of Justice warned that "every day the district court's order remains in effect, additional aliens will rush to seek classification and entry as an H-1B nonimmigrant worker."

Sorokin agreed to pause his ruling while the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit decides whether to intervene. The fee, in effect, remains in place for now.

The White House was blunt. "President Trump has clear legal authority to restrict entry of any class of aliens he determines is not in America's best interests, and that is exactly what he did," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said. Trump himself called the judges "crazy" for pushing back.

## Congress Steps In — On Both Sides

The court battle has now spilled into Capitol Hill. Republican Representative Mike Kennedy of Utah introduced the PROTECT Act the day after Sorokin's ruling, seeking to codify the $100,000 fee through legislation. "We needed somebody in Congress to actually take care of this," Kennedy told reporters.

But several Republican lawmakers from rural districts broke ranks, pointing out that the fee was devastating healthcare systems and small universities in their areas — institutions that have nothing to do with the big tech outsourcing debate that originally motivated the crackdown.

Meanwhile, a separate legal challenge in the District of Columbia produced the opposite result: Obama-appointed Judge Beryl Howell sided with the administration in December, finding the fee lawful. Additional challenges are pending in the Northern District of California.

## What Happens Next

The First Circuit's emergency stay decision will determine whether the fee comes back in full force or whether employers get a reprieve. Legal experts say the conflicting rulings — one judge striking it down, another upholding it — make it increasingly likely the Supreme Court will eventually weigh in.

For now, the practical effect is paralysis. Employers who paused their H-1B filings after Sorokin's ruling have no clarity on whether the $100,000 charge applies. Those who rushed to file new petitions during the brief window may find themselves facing the fee again if the appeals court sides with the government.

The case is *State of California v. Mullin*, No. 1:25-cv-13829, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts.
